extracted.intended_audience: employers, occupational safety and health professionals, and stakeholders responding to OSHA's heat standard proposal
extracted.subtask_description: Extracts employer obligations and implementation details from OSHA's proposed heat standard (NPRM) covering requirements at the initial and high heat triggers, emergency response, signage, and training. Focused on operational requirements, timing/frequency, and equipment/supplies employers must provide or actions they must take.

rubrics_metrics.name: Equipment requirements at or above the initial heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must provide certain equipment items when the initial heat trigger is met or exceeded (listed as equipment-based unit costs).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table VIII.C.14 lists items and unit costs assumed by OSHA: Coolers with Spigot (1.0 unit, $79.99, Employee, One-Time), Reusable Water Bottle (1.0, $0.59, Employee, One-Time), Outdoor Break Area Engineering Control (1.0, $119.99, Establishment, One-Time), Air Movement (2.0, $134.99 each, Employee, One-Time), Humidity Control (2.0, $39.19 each, Employee, One-Time). Sources and price bases are cited (Igloo, Amazon, DiscountMugs, WebstaurantStore).

rubrics_metrics.name: Rest breaks at the high heat trigger
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must provide a minimum of 15-minute paid rest breaks at least every two hours; a meal break may count as a rest break.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes two paid 15-minute rest breaks and an unpaid meal break per at-risk worker per 8-hour shift at or above the high heat trigger. The standard also requires if-needed rest breaks (as required at the initial trigger). Travel time to/from break area is accounted for (assumed 2 minutes indoor, 4 minutes outdoor per rest break). OSHA models productivity/pacing changes across three employee groups (Group 1: no current breaks; Group 2: if-needed breaks only; Group 3: already compliant) and estimates reductions in pacing/time-costs (detailed in table VIII.C.15 and appendix A). The rest break unit costs in table VIII.C.16 are reported without reflecting pacing-related cost savings offset.

rubrics_metrics.name: Observation for signs and symptoms of heat illness
rubrics_metrics.description: At or above the high heat trigger, employers must observe employees for signs and symptoms of heat-related illness, with specific compliance options.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Options include a mandatory buddy system, observation by a supervisor or heat safety coordinator, or communication with lone workers every 2 hours. OSHA assumes employers will use supervisors/heat safety coordinators (one observer per no more than 20 employees). Time estimates: 15 seconds of the designated person's time three times per employee per 8-hour shift that meets/exceeds the high heat trigger; similarly, each at-risk worker will spend 15 seconds three times per shift. Labor unit costs for observation (designated person and at-risk worker) are shown in table VIII.C.16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hazard alert (notifications to employees)
rubrics_metrics.description: When the high heat trigger is met or exceeded, employers must notify employees about hydration, right to breaks, heat emergency procedures, and locations of break areas and drinking water (including for mobile worksites).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates a designated person will spend 5 minutes one time per heat season preparing and delivering the first notification; subsequent notifications use the same format and take 30 seconds to update and resend for each 8-hour shift at or above the initial heat trigger. OSHA assumes employee time to review the hazard alert is negligible. Labor unit costs for initial and subsequent hazard alerts (supervisor time) are provided in tables VIII.C.16 (labor) and equipment/unit cost tables.

rubrics_metrics.name: Warning signs for excessively high heat areas (indoor)
rubrics_metrics.description: For indoor workplaces, employers must place warning signs at areas with ambient temperatures that regularly exceed 120°F.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes this applies only in certain industries with radiant heat sources (furnaces, hot water systems, ovens, smelting). Assumed average of 1.5 signs per establishment (1–2 signs). A designated person would take approximately 5 minutes to install each sign. Table VIII.C.17 shows equipment-based unit cost for Warning Signs: 1.5 units at $13.50 each = $20.25 total (one-time). Labor for signage placement (one-time) is shown in table VIII.C.16.

rubrics_metrics.name: Heat illness and emergency response planning (HIIPP inclusion)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must include a heat emergency response plan as part of their Heat Injury and Illness Prevention Program (HIIPP) and undertake required activities for any at-risk worker experiencing signs/symptoms of heat-related illness, with immediate action appropriate to severity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA requests comment on cooling methods but uses the U.S. Army recommended method for cost estimates. Requirements include: procedures for immediate action for suspected emergencies; monitoring non-emergency cases; contacting EMS for emergencies; transporting employees to EMS-accessible locations when necessary; and providing means to reduce body temperature on-site. OSHA provides assumed resource needs and unit costs (labor and equipment) for planning and response (tables VIII.C.18–VIII.C.19).

rubrics_metrics.name: Immediate and non-emergency medical response actions and timing
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific timing and actions employers must take when an employee shows signs of heat illness: monitoring for non-emergency cases and immediate cooling/EMS contact for emergencies.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA estimates: non-emergency monitoring requires a designated person to spend 45 minutes per incident; suspected heat emergency requires 12.5 minutes to reduce body temperature (based on Casa et al., 2007) plus an immediate 2-minute call to EMS. If the employee is in a location off a roadway requiring transport to EMS access, a designated person will spend about 30 minutes transporting the employee per incident. OSHA provides sector-specific labor unit-cost estimates for Medical Response—Non-Emergency, Medical Response—Emergency, Contact Emergency Medical Services, and Transport Worker in table VIII.C.18.

rubrics_metrics.name: On-site emergency cooling supplies and equipment
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must have equipment/supplies to reduce an employee's body temperature when necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: OSHA assumes employers will use two sets of four bed sheets wetted and cooled per employee, swapping every three minutes; assumes capacity for two simultaneous incidents. Thus, per establishment OSHA assumes 16 sheets (8 per individual to cool two individuals) and two coolers, plus six seven-pound bags of ice for each 8-hour shift that meets/exceeds the initial heat trigger. Table VIII.C.19 lists equipment unit costs and frequencies: Ice Sheets (16 units, $9.99 each, $159.84 total, one-time), Ice (6 units, $0.69 each, daily at initial trigger), Ice Cooler (2 units, $31.70 each, one-time). Sources: Amazon, Grainger, Walmart.

rubrics_metrics.name: Training program requirements (employees, supervisors, heat safety coordinators)
rubrics_metrics.description: Employers must develop and implement training programs for employees, supervisors, and heat safety coordinators, with specified timing and refresher/supplemental requirements.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Training is required initially (prior to work at/above the initial heat trigger), annually (refresher), and supplemental when necessary (after heat-related incidents, new tasks, or policy changes). OSHA assumes a designated person develops and implements training with the following estimates: For employee training—4 hours to develop initial program, 30 minutes to prepare initial sessions, 1 hour administering each initial session; employees spend 1 hour for initial training and 30 minutes for each refresher. For supervisor/heat safety coordinator training—4 hours development, 15 minutes preparation, 1 hour to deliver initial training; supervisors/heat safety coordinators attend 1 hour initial and 30 minutes for refresher. Supplemental training: designated person 15 minutes prep and 30 minutes to conduct; employees attend 30 minutes. OSHA assumes supplemental training will be conducted by 1% of establishments each year and 1% of employees will attend. Table VIII.C.20 provides sector-by-sector labor unit cost estimates for development, preparation, delivery, and attendance (initial, refresher, supervisor-specific).

rubrics_metrics.name: Labor-unit cost and frequency reporting for high-heat requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: OSHA reports labor-based unit costs (hours and dollar unit costs) by industry sector for the various required activities at or above the high heat trigger.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Table VIII.C.16 and Table VIII.C.18 present sector-specific hours and unit-cost estimates for activities including Rest Breaks (indoor/outdoor), Observation for Signs and Symptoms (designated person and at-risk worker), Initial and Subsequent Hazard Alerts (supervisor), Signage Placement (one-time), Medical Response (non-emergency and emergency), Contact EMS, Transport Worker, and training labor categories. Each line shows sector code, hours, unit cost, labor category, basis (employee, establishment, incident), and frequency (daily at high heat trigger, one-time, annual, incident). These are OSHA's cost-estimation parameters rather than new procedural options.
